---
name: accounting
description: "The dashboard, its cells, the runs' records and transcripts, and how cost and time are derived. Read before filling dashboard cells or collecting a run's records."
---

# Accounting

What a campaign records about its own work: the dashboard, the runs' records and
transcripts its figures come from, and how cost and time are derived from them.

## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

## 3. Records

Every run's `task.json` records how its agent ran: its backend, billing, model proxy and
the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the
name its host gives its transcript, under the spawning session's `subagents/`.

A transcript is copied into crustify's home, as `transcripts/<session id>.jsonl`, as soon
as its agent ends, because the CLIs move and prune their own files. Its usage is derived
from the copy, as [`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) describes, with the backend and model proxy its
`task.json` names.

An evolution review is a run like any other: its `task.json` sits in its artifact dir, and
its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

## 4. Cost and time

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

An agent's wall time is its usage's interval. A wave's runs from its first batch's
launch through its final review and regression gates, a review wave's in an audit through
its landing, and a module's from its first launch through its final gate.

name: versioning
description: "Repositories, branches, worktrees, landing under the landing lock, promotion, integration, their lifecycle, and the identity every commit takes. Read before the first commit, and before creating, landing on, promoting or purging any branch or worktree."
---

# Versioning

How a campaign's work is held in version control: the repositories it works in, their
branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Repositories

A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
inside it.

| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
|---|---|---|
| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |

`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.

An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.

## 2. Branches

| branch | name | checked out |
|---|---|---|
| shipping | `main` in the campaign's own repository; `crustify/main` in an audit, beside the reviewed crate's own branches | never while the campaign runs |
| working | `crustify/devel` | in the repository's base dir |
| planner run | `crustify/planner/run-<n>` | in the repository's base dir, while its run is live |
| module | `crustify/modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or `crustify/foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module | in its worktree, while it integrates |
| wave | `crustify/waves/wave-<index>` | never |
| batch | `crustify/batches/wave-<index>/batch-<index>` | in its worktree |

The shipping branch holds what the user has approved to ship: it advances only with the
user's approval, by a fast-forward to the working branch, and each advance is tagged on it,
`ship-<n>` numbered from 1, or `crustify/ship-<n>` in an audit. The working branch is where the
campaign integrates its work: planner runs fork from it and are promoted back to it, and
the modules are integrated into it, as `scheduling` describes.

A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
another, so no two module branches collide.

A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.

An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
way.

## 3. Worktrees

Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as
[`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s Ids section names them, so that its name tells which
module it works on, and so does a module while it integrates, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/integration`, beside its batches'. A
planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.

## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.

### 4.4 Progress

The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.

### 4.5 Integration

A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.

1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.

## 5. Lifecycle

Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
only it needed is purged.

### 5.1 Campaign

The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.

The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to
it, so that every promotion and integration is a fast-forward: the progress recorded in
the meantime stays in the base checkout's working tree until then, as
[Progress](#44-progress) describes.

### 5.2 Planner runs

A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.

### 5.3 Modules

A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.

A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

### 5.4 Waves

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
requires; that commit is the wave's base.
Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
describes, and its branch purged.

A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records, since no batch changes the C.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

## 3. Records

Every run's `task.json` records how its agent ran: its backend, billing, model proxy and
the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the
name its host gives its transcript, under the spawning session's `subagents/`.

A transcript is copied into crustify's home, as `transcripts/<session id>.jsonl`, as soon
as its agent ends, because the CLIs move and prune their own files. Its usage is derived
from the copy, as [`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) describes, with the backend and model proxy its
`task.json` names.

An evolution review is a run like any other: its `task.json` sits in its artifact dir, and
its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

## 4. Cost and time

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

An agent's wall time is its usage's interval. A wave's runs from its first batch's
launch through its final review and regression gates, a review wave's in an audit through
its landing, and a module's from its first launch through its final gate.

name: versioning
description: "Repositories, branches, worktrees, landing under the landing lock, promotion, integration, their lifecycle, and the identity every commit takes. Read before the first commit, and before creating, landing on, promoting or purging any branch or worktree."

# Versioning

How a campaign's work is held in version control: the repositories it works in, their
branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Repositories

A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
inside it.

| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
|---|---|---|
| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |

`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.

An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.

## 2. Branches

| branch | name | checked out |
|---|---|---|
| shipping | `main` in the campaign's own repository; `crustify/main` in an audit, beside the reviewed crate's own branches | never while the campaign runs |
| working | `crustify/devel` | in the repository's base dir |
| planner run | `crustify/planner/run-<n>` | in the repository's base dir, while its run is live |
| module | `crustify/modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or `crustify/foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module | in its worktree, while it integrates |
| wave | `crustify/waves/wave-<index>` | never |
| batch | `crustify/batches/wave-<index>/batch-<index>` | in its worktree |

The shipping branch holds what the user has approved to ship: it advances only with the
user's approval, by a fast-forward to the working branch, and each advance is tagged on it,
`ship-<n>` numbered from 1, or `crustify/ship-<n>` in an audit. The working branch is where the
campaign integrates its work: planner runs fork from it and are promoted back to it, and
the modules are integrated into it, as `scheduling` describes.

A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
another, so no two module branches collide.

A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.

An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
way.

## 3. Worktrees

Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as
[`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s Ids section names them, so that its name tells which
module it works on, and so does a module while it integrates, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/integration`, beside its batches'. A
planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.

## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.

### 4.4 Progress

The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.

### 4.5 Integration

A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.

1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.

## 5. Lifecycle

Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
only it needed is purged.

### 5.1 Campaign

The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.

The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to
it, so that every promotion and integration is a fast-forward: the progress recorded in
the meantime stays in the base checkout's working tree until then, as
[Progress](#44-progress) describes.

### 5.2 Planner runs

A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.

### 5.3 Modules

A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.

A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

### 5.4 Waves

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
requires; that commit is the wave's base.
Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
describes, and its branch purged.

A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records, since no batch changes the C.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.

content.content: --- name: ffibox description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one." --- # ffibox ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a value; what C does not alias is plain Rust. Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md` describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes. What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there. ## Planning ### Dependencies › Adopted crates A candidate crate's soundness is read against the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists, each of which ffibox excludes from the campaign's own bindings: the crate qualifies where its safe API excludes them too, by whatever means it uses. ## Binding workflow ### Binding workflow › Rust tree The workspace depends on ffibox by path, on the checkout the host provides, which is on the campaign's working branch of it, `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }` in Crustify's image, so that each run records its revision among its task's `revisions`. The path is the checkout's canonical one, with no symbolic link on it, and a `[patch]` that redirects another source of ffibox names the same: compile-fail snapshots normalize a path dependency only where the compiler's paths match the dependency's canonical directory. ## Binding and porting Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`, `docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too. ### Binding types A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them. ### Binding types › Safe layout While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox;`, and `CArc` for `FooArc`. A value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal`. ### Binding symbols › Functions A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them. ### Binding symbols › Function pointers A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier, `callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body. A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a `CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as `docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table. ### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C. ### Porting › FFI boundary An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does with the Rust it reaches: - the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`, `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return its owners and handles; - memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C frees it through an exported release; - a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a `CPayload`; and - the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`. ### Porting types › Structs Until a ported struct's `port/layout`, its handles are ffibox's, as [Binding types › Safe layout](#binding-types--safe-layout) describes; from it on, `FooRef` and `FooMut` are aliases of native borrows. Its owners stay ffibox's until its `port/memory`, or until its `port/layout` where that comes first, as below, their policy calling its lifecycle routines, C's through their raw bindings until each is ported, then the Rust ones. A `port/memory` before its `port/layout` keeps them ffibox's and changes their policy to `RustAlloc` alone: `FooBox` becomes `CBox`, its handles unchanged, until its `port/layout` makes it `Box`, or `Pin>` while C keeps its address. Between a struct's `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, its layout is native while C still allocates or frees its storage, and ffibox's single-object owners, which hold only C-layout types, cannot hold it. Where C releases it with its allocation family's free alone, and the native type is not zero-sized and needs no drop (`size_of::() != 0` and `!core::mem::needs_drop::()`, both asserted at compile time), and C does not keep its address, `FooBox` is `Box>` and a counted run of them `Vec>`, `P` the family's `Copy` policy with the alignment the family guarantees: an existing `CLenAlloc` policy of the family, or one declared with `impl_clenalloc!`'s `align =`. A box is built with `CAllocator::try_box`, which refuses an over-aligned type at compile time and returns C's out-of-memory failure, and handed to C with `Box::into_raw_with_allocator`; a run grows with `Vec::try_reserve`, keeping C's out-of-memory failure, and is handed to C through `CVec::try_from` and `into_raw_parts`. A pointer C hands back is adopted with `Box::from_raw_in`, under the conditions `CBox::into_box`'s documentation lists, and a run with `Vec::from_raw_parts_in`, its length as its capacity, under the allocator's fit rule. Its `port/memory` makes them `Box` and `Vec`. ## Testing ### Testing › UB tests The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test. ## Reviewing Reviewing reads `docs/goals.md`. ### Reviewing › Objectives A workset's use of ffibox's primitives is reviewed against ffibox's documentation, and its hand-written representations against the contract ffibox would have enforced. # ffibox

Generic smart pointers and traits for building safe Rust wrappers over C
types and pointers, in both directions: memory C owns, held from Rust, and
memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Designed for arbitrary
user-space C interop, including the case where you need direct field access
and a C-ABI-compatible layout (porting C internals to Rust in place), not just
opaque-handle wrapping.

## Why

Wrapping a C API in Rust means re-homing C's ownership and lifecycle
conventions into RAII. The recurring shapes:

- A C-allocated object with a destructor (`free`), and maybe a copy (`dup`).
- A constructor or allocator (`foo_alloc`, `malloc`, `calloc`) whose result
  must be released by its paired free.
- A refcounted object shared by several holders (`up_ref` / `unref`), maybe
  with a C lock over the state they mutate.
- Types with multiple or runtime-conditional destructors.
- A by-value struct whose teardown disposes its fields but not the struct.
- An owned length-aware buffer or NUL-terminated `char *` with a C destructor.
- A type-erased `void *` that stays opaque end to end.

Each shape gets one owner type, generic over a **policy** — a type you declare
that names the C routines. `impl_cdrop!` and its siblings bind a C routine to a
policy; a type alias names the pair: `pub type FooBox = CBox<Foo, FooFree>;`.

## Mental model in one paragraph

No reference to C-owned memory is formed while anything may write or free it:
objects are reached through handles, and only a run of bytes nothing writes
while it is lent is a `&CStr` or `&[u8]`. Each C type gets a layout type
`Foo` (`#[repr(transparent)]` over `ffi::foo`; `Foo<'r>` when the C object
borrows its parent) and two borrowed handles, `FooRef<'a>` / `FooMut<'a>`,
each one pointer wide and carrying the getters and setters; field access projects a raw pointer out of the handle. Ownership

That is right for an allocator any thread may free into (`free`, a library's `lib_free`); for one that must free on the allocating thread, opt out by giving the policy a `PhantomData<*const ()>` field. ## Choosing an owner: what shape is the owned thing? Reached once dropping the Rust value is what releases the object. When it is not, the answer is a borrow instead — see [borrows.md](borrows.md#choosing-a-borrow). - **A NUL-terminated string** (`char *`, no stored length) → `CStrBox

`. `strlen` recovers the length, so one `CDrop` policy covers a plain free and a clearing free alike. Its views are read-only, like `CStr`. - **A counted array** → `CVec`, one policy per allocator family. Plain elements (`CPlainElem`: integers, floats, raw pointers, `MaybeUninit`) and owners (`CSliceElem`) read out as a real `&[T]` because the buffer is exclusively owned; wrapped C objects come out as handles through `as_handles` → `CSlice`, since `&[Foo]` would cover them. Where C returns NULL with 0 for an empty array, adopt with `from_raw_parts_or_empty`; plain `from_raw_parts` treats every NULL as failure. Dropping a `CVec` drops its elements, as a `Vec` does, so the element type says what each slot owns. A wrapper around a `CVec` therefore never drops the elements itself: a `Drop` that does frees each one twice. Up to ffibox 0.1.1 a `CVec` freed the buffer alone, and code written for that is migrated as the [CHANGELOG](../CHANGELOG.md) describes. | C array | element type | |---------|--------------| | `foo **`, each entry owned, NULL allowed | `Option>` | | `char **`, each string owned | `Option>` | | `foo *`, each inline value disposed | `CVal` | | freed with its elements by one routine (`foo_array_free(arr, n)`) | an owner from the rows above, under the array allocator's policy, not that routine | | entries borrowed from elsewhere | the bare pointer | The element type releases the elements, and the policy the array alone: `CLenDrop::c_drop_len` frees the buffer after the `CVec` has dropped every element. So a routine that frees both is never the `CLenDrop`. Over owner elements it frees each a second time; over bare pointers, which are `CPlainElem`, the `CVec` derefs to `&mut [*mut foo]`, through which safe code stores any pointer, or NULL, in a slot the routine then frees; and the policy, a public type, also frees the buffer of a `CVec` of any other element type, whose bytes the routine would read as `foo *`s. Where the routine's body is only those frees, as libgit2's `git_strlist_free` is (`git__free` on each string, then on the array), a `CVec>, GitFree>` releases the same way on drop and the routine is not called. Where it does more, the wrapper is hand-written — see [hand-written.md](hand-written.md#an-array-freed-by-one-routine). Adopting a buffer of owners (`from_raw_parts` and its siblings) asserts that each non-null element is an allocation of its own: a pointer repeated in two slots is freed twice. - **One object held inline** — a local, a field, an array element, with no pointer of its own: - owns no resources → the `Foo` itself (`Foo::zeroed()` when it is `CZeroable`, or a wrapper constructor that has C fill a local); - owns resources and stands alone → `CVal`; - embedded in a parent C struct → a bare `Foo`, disposed by the parent's teardown (a `Drop` on it would dispose twice); - address-sensitive (points into itself, or C recorded its address) → not inline at all: behind a pointer, as below. - **One object behind a pointer** → `CBox` if this is the only reference, `CArc` if it is one of several counted ones. `CBox` owns only `CCell` layout types, from `define_ctype!` or written by hand, as does `CArc`: a `void *` payload is bytes (`CVec`) or a typed owner of its own. ## Policies — what teardown means Every owner's destructor is a **policy**: a type you declare, usually a unit struct deriving `Clone, Copy, Debug, Default`, implementing the lifecycle traits. Bind a C routine to it with the `impl_*!` macros, or implement the traits by hand when teardown needs runtime state. A unit struct is `Send + Sync`, which makes a `CStrBox` or plain-element `CVec` under it free on whichever thread drops it; a thread-bound allocator's policy carries `PhantomData<*const ()>` instead (see [Thread safety](#conventions) above). | Trait | Defines | Macro | Drives | |-------|---------|-------|--------| | `CDrop` | `c_drop` — a `*_free`, or a refcount down-ref | `impl_cdrop!(P, Foo, f)`; `_str` for `c_char` | `CBox`, `CStrBox`, `CArc` | | `CDupClone: CDrop` | `c_dup` — a deep copy (a NEW pointer, NULL on failure) | `impl_cdupclone!(P, Foo, f)`; `_str` for `strdup` | `Clone` / `try_clone` | | `CRefClone: CDrop` | `c_up_ref` — a refcount increment on the SAME pointer; `c_is_sole_owner` (default `false`) | `impl_crefclone!(P, Foo, f)`; `…, ok = |r| r == 1`, `…, sole = g` | `CArc`'s `Clone`, `get_mut`, `make_mut` | | `CLenDrop` | `c_drop_len` — a buffer free, given the byte length; the buffer only, never its elements | `impl_clendrop!(P, f)` | `CVec` | | `CLenClone: CLenDrop` | `c_clone_len` — a buffer memdup (`T: Copy` only) from any readable source; `ALIGN` (default 1) bounds the element types it can copy | `impl_clenclone!(P, f)`, `impl_clenclone!(P, f, align = 16)` | `CVec`'s `Clone`, `CVec::from_slice`, `CSlice::to_cvec` | | `CLenAlloc: CLenDrop` | `c_alloc_len` — uninitialised buffer storage (`malloc(n)`); `ALIGN` as above; `c_realloc_len` — `realloc`, provided as `malloc`, copy and `free` | `impl_clenalloc!(P, f)`, `…, align = 16`, `…, realloc = g` | `CVec::from_fn`, `CVec::new_uninit`, `CAllocator

` | | `CDispose` | `c_dispose` — `*_uninit` / `*_clear` on a value | `impl_cdispose!(P, Foo, f)` | `CVal` | | `CNew: CDrop` | `c_new` — a zero-argument `*_alloc` / `*_new` | by hand | `CBox::new`, `CArc::new` | | `CAlloc: CDrop + CDrop>` | `c_alloc` — uninitialised storage (`malloc`); the free must not read it | by hand | `CBox::new_uninit` | | `CAllocZeroed: CDrop` | `c_alloc_zeroed` — zero-filled storage (`calloc`) | by hand | `CBox::new_zeroed`, `CArc::new_zeroed` | | `CZeroable`, on `Foo` | all-zero is valid for every accessor, safe wrapper and paired teardown; provides `Foo::zeroed()` | `unsafe impl CZeroable for Foo {}` | `new_zeroed`, `Foo::zeroed()` | | `CGuarded`, on `Foo` | `c_lock` / `c_unlock`; the `Locked` handle; the `Scope` it covers | `impl_cguarded!(Foo, FooLocked, lock = f, unlock = g)`; `…, ok = |r| r == 1`; `impl_cguarded!(Foo, all, …)` for `CGuardedAll` | `CArc::lock`, `CGuardedRef::lock` | `Foo` in the Macro column is any `CCell` layout type, `define_ctype!`'s or hand-written; one that carries a lifetime is written `Foo<'_>`, as **A layout type with a lifetime** below describes, in every macro but `impl_cdupclone!` and `impl_cguarded!`, which name it in a leading list: `<'r> P, Foo<'r>`. **Because the policy is a type parameter, an owner cannot exist without a destructor, and one C type can have several.** `CBox` next to `CBox`: exactly one ever runs per box, chosen by its type. And since each clone trait sits on the same policy as the drop trait, a `*_dup` is always settled by its `*_free`. **`CBox` is a sole owner; `CArc` shares.** `CBox::as_mut` hands out the exclusive handle, which is sound only while nothing else uses the object, so `CBox` clones only by deep copy. A refcounted object fits a `CBox` while the box holds its only reference (with the down-ref as `c_drop`); `CArc::from` shares it, and `CBox::try_from` (or `try_into_box`) takes it back once the count is 1 again. **Shared and mutable means locked — usually, part of it.** A `CArc` has no unlocked write path: its exclusive handle needs the count to prove the reference sole (`get_mut`, which needs `c_is_sole_owner` — an Acquire read of a count that covers every reference, C's own included), or a private copy (`make_mut`, through `CDupClone` — never a byte copy, which would duplicate the object's sub-allocations, its count and its lock). A C object rarely locks all of itself: it locks the state its holders mutate — a cache, a list of backends — and leaves the rest fixed once set up. That is `Arc` with a `Mutex` field, not `Arc>`, and the handles split the same way: | State | Handle | Reached through | |-------|--------|-----------------| | fixed once shared; routines that lock internally | `FooRef` | `CArc::as_ref()`, always | | protected by the lock — reads too; routines that need it held | `FooLocked` | `CArc::lock()` → `CGuard::as_locked()` | | anything | `FooMut` | `CArc::get_mut()`, sole reference only | A getter for protected state never goes on `FooRef`: it would race with a writer holding the lock through another clone. `CGuarded`'s contract makes C take or require the same lock, and makes the layout type invariant in any lifetime the protected state can hold (as a `Mutex` field does), so a covariant `CArc` cannot shrink one. The lock must not be recursive: a second `lock` on the same thread blocks forever, or panics when the lock reports the self-deadlock (`EDEADLK`), rather than hand out a second `FooLocked`. A failing C lock call panics, as `std`'s locks do; there is no poisoning. An object whose lock covers all of it is `CGuardedAll` (`impl_cguarded!(Foo, all, …)`): its locked handle is `FooMut`, so it is reached only through a `CGuardedRef`, which has no unlocked path, and `CArc::lock` rejects it at compile time. **Routines are plain paths, type-checked.** Each macro calls the routine with a pointer of the exact C type; a routine for the wrong type does not compile. Where a call can fail — an up_ref, a lock — the routine either returns `()` or is bound with `ok = |r| r == 1` (whatever its success value is); a status code is never silently discarded, so `pthread_mutex_lock`'s `EDEADLK` becomes a panic rather than a second locked handle. A routine of any other shape — a destructor taking the slot (`ffi::foo_free(&mut p)`), an up_ref or a copy that answers through an out-parameter (`ffi::foo_dup(&mut out, p)`), a `void *` allocator free, extra arguments — goes behind a small `unsafe fn` adapter passed to the macro by path. The adapter is private, with a `# Safety` section of its own, and sits beside the policy it serves, where the crate keeps its unsafe code (its unsafe region, if it has one), as a hand-written impl would. Prefer it to a hand-written `unsafe impl CDrop` (or `CRefClone`, `CDupClone`): the macro keeps the impl's shape and its type check of the C pointer, and the adapter adds no public unsafe surface, only a private `unsafe fn` and the unsafe block calling the routine, which a hand-written impl holds too. Teardown is unconditional: a gate that suppresses it on some paths folds into the routine itself. **A layout type with a lifetime.** A layout type that carries a lifetime, `Blob<'r>` over an object that keeps its repository, whether `define_ctype!` declares it or it is written by hand, takes its policies from the macros: `impl_cdrop!`, `impl_crefclone!` and `impl_cdispose!` accept it with the lifetime spelled `'_`, which the impl header turns into a parameter, so one policy serves `Blob<'r>` for every `'r`. A named lifetime (`Blob<'r>`) is undeclared there and does not compile. ```rust,ignore impl_cdrop!(BlobFree, Blob<'_>, ffi::blob_free); // `blob_dup` answers through an out-parameter: an adapter gives it the shape. impl_crefclone!(BlobFree, Blob<'_>, blob_up_ref, ok = |r| r == 0); pub type BlobArc<'r> = CArc, BlobFree>; ``` Two macros take the lifetime named instead, in a list ahead of their arguments. `impl_cdupclone!`'s `c_dup` returns the type, and a `'_` there elides to `&self`'s lifetime rather than the parameter's; `impl_cguarded!` names the type in a struct and an associated type, where `'_` is not allowed. ```rust,ignore impl_cdupclone!(<'r> BlobFree, Blob<'r>, ffi::blob_copy); impl_cguarded!(<'r> Cache<'r>, CacheLocked, lock = ffi::cache_lock, unlock = ffi::cache_unlock); // CacheLocked<'a, 'r>, the handle a held lock grants ``` A layout type generic over a type, rather than a lifetime, has no elided form: all its policies are hand-written. [examples.md](examples.md#a-layout-type-with-a-lifetime--define_ctype-with-phantom) shows the whole wrapper. **Runtime-state policies.** When teardown needs a value chosen at the wrapping site (`list_pop_free(list, elem_free_fn)`, `pool_free(pool, p)`), write the policy by hand — a struct holding the state, implementing `CDrop` (and `CDupClone` + `Clone` to clone) — and hold the object in a `CBoxState`, which stores the policy beside the pointer. Adopt with `from_raw_with(ptr, ElemFree(f))` and release with `into_raw_with()`. `CBox`, `CArc` and `CStrBox` hold a stateless policy, so that each is the pointer it stands in for; one with state fails to build in them. A routine known at compile time needs no state: a unit-struct policy per routine names it. **Construction goes through the policy too.** Bind a constructor to the policy and the owner's type pairs allocation with teardown, just as it pairs `*_dup` with `*_free`. A safely built `CBox` was allocated by `P`, and `from_raw` is the only way around that, which is why it is `unsafe`. - `CNew` is a type's own zero-argument constructor (`frame_alloc`). Constructors that take arguments stay inherent functions on `Foo` returning a `CBox`, because a trait signature cannot carry their parameters. - `CAllocZeroed` asks for zero-filled storage and needs `Foo: CZeroable`. That marker means all-zero is a state every safe accessor, every safe wrapper and the paired teardown accept, not merely a valid Rust value. Leave it off a type whose C constructor sets non-zero defaults. - `CAlloc` gives uninitialised storage, which C fills through `as_c_ptr` and the caller promotes with `unsafe assume_init`. Because a box dropped before that point frees through `CDrop>`, the policy's free must not read the object, so a destructor like `frame_free` cannot implement it. **The construction phase.** An allocation that is still being filled in is held under a storage-only policy, either `new_uninit` or a hand-written `CBox`, and then promoted with `with_policy(FooFree)` once it satisfies the full destructor. Bail with `?` before promoting and only the storage is freed. ## Choosing a policy For boxes, strings and buffers. | C routines | Policy | |------------|--------| | `foo_free` | `impl_cdrop!` | | `foo_alloc()` + `foo_free` | `impl_cdrop!` + a hand-written `CNew` → `CBox::new()` | | `malloc` / `realloc` + `free`, an allocation family | `impl_clendrop!` + `impl_clenalloc!` on one policy `P`; `CAllocator

` is then the storage-only policy of every owner (`CBox`, `CStrBox`, `CVec`) and the `Allocator` of `Box` / `Vec` | | `malloc` / `calloc` + `free`, for any type, without a family | a generic hand-written `CDrop` + `CAlloc` / `CAllocZeroed` | | `foo_free` + `foo_dup` | `impl_cdrop!` + `impl_cdupclone!` | | `foo_unref`, held as the only reference | `impl_cdrop!` with the down-ref; no `Clone` | | `foo_unref` + `foo_up_ref`, shared, read-only | `impl_cdrop!` + `impl_crefclone!` → `CArc` | | … and a readable count | `impl_crefclone!(…, sole = g)`: `get_mut` without a copy | | … with state every holder mutates under a C lock | + `impl_cguarded!(Foo, FooLocked, …)` → `CArc::lock`; protected getters and setters on `FooLocked` | | a global, never freed, under one C lock | no policy: `impl_cguarded!(Foo, all, …)` → `CGuardedRef<'static, Foo>` | | a counted reference with no up_ref | `impl_cdrop!` alone → `CArc` without `Clone` | | teardown needs runtime state | a hand-written policy; adopt with `from_raw_with` | | built in place, not by a C constructor | `CAlloc` → `new_uninit` → `assume_init`, then `with_policy` if a fuller destructor takes over | | a routine of another shape: a slot, an out-parameter, extra arguments | the macro, over a private `unsafe fn` adapter passed by path, not a hand-written impl | | any of the above, over a layout type with a lifetime (`Blob<'r>`) | the same macros with `Blob<'_>`, but a hand-written `CDupClone` and `CGuarded` | | Rust allocates it (`alloc` feature) | `RustAlloc`: objects, buffers and strings from Rust's global allocator | An owned pointer crosses the FFI boundary on the owner's raw seam: `into_raw` surrenders it to C, `from_raw` adopts one C allocated, and `from_c_out` / `from_raw_out` adopt one a C routine returns through an out-parameter. `RustAlloc` is the policy over Rust's global allocator. An object or buffer Rust allocates is held by the same owners and handles as one C allocated, and when a type's allocation moves from C to Rust during a port, only its owner's alias changes: `CBox` becomes `CBox`. What it allocates only it frees; [outbound.md](outbound.md) covers offering it to C. ## `Box` and `Vec` over a C allocator A C allocation family, `malloc` / `realloc` / `free` and the alignment they vouch for, is a `CLenAlloc` policy, declared once: ```rust,ignore #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Default)] pub struct LibAlloc; impl_clendrop!(LibAlloc, lib_buf_free); // adapter over `lib_free(void *)` impl_clenalloc!(LibAlloc, ffi::lib_malloc, align = 16, realloc = ffi::lib_realloc); pub type LibAllocator = CAllocator; pub type LibBox = Box; pub type LibVec = Vec; pub type FooBox = CBox; // storage-only: `lib_free` releases it ``` A policy that already implements `CLenAlloc` by hand needs nothing more (an `Allocator` takes a `Copy` one, which has no drop to unwind; a unit struct is): `CAllocator

` over it is the standard `core::alloc::Allocator` (what `System` and `Global` are for Rust's heap), and a storage-only policy for `CBox`, `CStrBox` and `CVec`, as `RustAlloc` is over Rust's heap. **Which owner.** Both hold memory of the family; what decides is what C does with the value beyond its storage. | the value | owner | |-----------|-------| | a Rust value (a native-layout struct, a run of plain data or owners) whose storage C allocates or frees, and nothing more: C keeps no pointer into it while Rust holds it | `Box>`, `Vec>` | | a buffer Rust grows (`push`, `extend`, `try_reserve`) before handing it to C, or one C allocated that Rust grows | `Vec>`, into a `CVec` to hand over | | a C object reached through handles (a `CCell` layout type), or one C keeps a pointer to, or one address-sensitive | `CBox` | | released by a C lifecycle routine, not only `free` (`foo_free` disposing fields, a down-ref) | `CBox`, `CArc`: no `Allocator` releases it | | a counted object, a string | `CArc`, `CStrBox`: std's `Arc::new_in` and `String` with an allocator are not stable yet | | pinned, its address recorded by C | `CBox`: `Pin>` needs `StaticAllocator`, not stable yet | **Crossing.** The conversions keep the pointer and the allocator and copy nothing, where the owner's policy is `CAllocator
